name: Port Zante
label: Port Zante
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Port Zante' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Cruise terminal and waterfront shopping area.

text.description:
Port Zante is the cruise port at the heart of Basseterre, the capital of Saint Kitts and Nevis. It sits in the middle of Basseterre Bay on about 15 acres of land reclaimed from the sea in 1995, so it feels like a small waterfront quarter pushed out into the water. Its photo appeal is simple: big ships tied up at the piers, blue Caribbean water, and the island of Nevis as a backdrop. The green hills that wrap around the town add colour behind you when you turn round.

The best view is from the promenade along the berthed piers, looking out over the ships. The port's own guide also points to the entrance arch and the green-roofed plaza buildings, which make good close-up and street-scene shots. Two large ships can berth at once, and the port gets busy on arrival days, so try to shoot between arrivals if you can.

For a wider picture, the waterfront near the Treasury Building gives a view across the harbour that takes in the cruise berths and the town together. It is a good second shot if you have time.

Basseterre itself was founded by the French in 1627, which makes it one of the older towns in the Eastern Caribbean. Give yourself a few minutes to walk the length of the promenade, as the angle on the ships changes as you go.
text.geographic_location: Port Zante is in the centre of Basseterre Bay, on the waterfront of Basseterre, the capital of Saint Kitts. It is the town's cruise port.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give you here. If you are not arriving by ship, start from The Circus, the tourist centre of Basseterre, and head for the bay waterfront, where the port sits in the middle of the bay. Cruise passengers can walk straight off the ship onto the promenade. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a whole ship and the length of the pier into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the entrance arch and the green-roofed plaza buildings. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Nevis on the horizon behind the ships.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Port Zante, on the promenade along the berthed cruise piers, and look out over the ships.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the ship's waterline along a lower grid line so the sea and sky are balanced. Keep the horizon level. Leave a little water in front of the ship so it does not look cramped against the edge of the picture. For a different view, walk to the waterfront near the Treasury Building for a wider shot across the harbour that takes in the berths and the town together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ship's hull to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the white paint keeps its detail. Wipe the lens first, as sea air leaves a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Shoot between ship arrivals, when the promenade is quieter and the berths are clearer. Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and cooler colour than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The port gets busy on arrival days when two large ships are berthed, so expect more people on the promenade then.
claims_not_in_sources: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light than midday.
Sea air can leave a film on a phone lens.

name: Independence Square
label: Independence Square
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24800627: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Independence Square' (168 m across).
notes: Shaded historic park square at the heart of town.

text.description:
Independence Square is an open public square in the middle of Basseterre. It was first called Pall Mall Square, and the Government acquired it in 1750. It soon became the administrative, commercial and social centre of the town. It was renamed to mark St Kitts and Nevis becoming independent on 19 September 1983.

The square also has a painful past. It was a place where enslaved men, women and children were sold, on the spot where the fountain now stands. On the south side of the square, a building has a basement with barred windows that is still visible today. It is thought to have been used as an auction house. It is worth taking a quiet moment here before you start photographing.

On a phone, the square works best as a wide, open scene. The fountain gives you a natural centre point, and the buildings on the south side can frame the view. Stand back and let the space show, then move closer for details such as the fountain and the barred basement windows. Walk around a little, because the view changes as you move, and small changes in position can keep passers-by out of the frame. Take your time and be respectful if other visitors are reading or reflecting.
text.geographic_location: Independence Square is in the centre of Basseterre, in Saint George Basseterre Parish, on the island of Saint Kitts. It was the administrative, commercial and social centre of Basseterre.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed nearby, and the square is in Basseterre. From there, the middle of the square is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the fountain and the buildings on the south side. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on the south side, such as the barred basement windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the fountain on a crossing point rather than dead centre. Keep the horizon level and the building edges upright. Include a little foreground, such as paving or planting, to give a sense of depth. For a detail shot, use the telephoto to isolate the barred windows of the basement on the south side, and keep the frame simple and unposed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fountain or the buildings on the south side to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings do not turn too dark. Use the ultra-wide sparingly: keep the phone level, as tilting it will bend the buildings at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, but the square can be photographed at any time of day.

text.access_note: Independence Square is an open public square; if you want to go inside any of the buildings on the square, check the official site before you go.

name: Government House, Basseterre
label: Government House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Independence Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Independence Square' (way/24800627): middle (168 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/398547811: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Government House' (68 m across).

text.description: Government House, also known as Springfield House, is the official residence of the governor-general of Saint Kitts and Nevis, so it is a place to photograph from the outside rather than to explore. The site has a long story. In 1837 Thomas Harper took on a twenty-five acre lot, renamed it Springfield and built a house there. In 1848 the first archdeacon of St Kitts, Francis Robert Brathwaite, bought it. It later housed a series of rectors, and in 1946 the then governor, Sir Frederick Albert Phillip, moved in. The colonial-style main façade, seen from the street, is the picture most visitors want. It is a shaded, relaxed place for a quieter shot, and it is a good first stop on a walk across town. Government House is a fair way off to the west and will not be in your frame from the square, so treat the square as a pleasant photo in its own right and then walk on to the house. When you reach the house, stay on the public street and keep to what you can see from there. Take a few frames from slightly different positions, as a straight-on view and a slight angle give quite different results.
text.geographic_location: Government House lies roughly a kilometre west of Independence Square.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops serve this part of Basseterre. From Independence Square, head west across town to Government House, which is about a kilometre on foot. Check the way on your phone map as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: At the square, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole sweep of trees, fountain and old buildings, and the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. At Government House, the default lens (1x) suits the façade, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) lets you pick out detail from the pavement without stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Independence Square. A grassy, tree-lined square with its fountain and the older colonial buildings around its edges; no page confirms that Government House is in the frame from here. The photo from here shows the grassy, tree-lined square, its fountain and the older colonial buildings around the edges. Government House lies to the west, a walk away, and is not in this view. For the house itself, walk west and shoot its main façade from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: In the square, put the fountain or a tree-lined path in the foreground and let the colonial buildings fill the background. Switch on gridlines to keep the horizon level. At Government House, stand square on to the façade from the street, keep the building centred, and leave a little sky above the roofline. Take a second frame from a slight angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so white walls do not wash out. In the shady square, tap a mid-tone area so the dappled light stays natural.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings or late afternoons are usually kinder than midday, when the light is harsh and shadows are short. The shade in the square helps if you are there around noon.

text.access_note: Government House is an official residence, so view and photograph it from the public street and check the official site before you go in case any visits are possible.
claims_not_in_sources: Government House lies roughly a kilometre west of Independence Square.
Government House will not be visible in photos taken from Independence Square.
Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light than midday.
The façade can be photographed from the public street.

name: National Museum of Saint Kitts
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bay Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bay Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/398248819: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum' (41 m across).
notes: Historic Treasury Building on the waterfront near the Circus.

text.description:
The National Museum of Saint Kitts occupies a handsome colonial building on Bay Road in Basseterre. It was built in 1894 as the Treasury Building and was once the entry point for people arriving from the nearby pier. The treasury moved to a new building in 1996, and the museum opened here in 2002. It is run by the St. Christopher National Trust and covers the culture and heritage of Saint Kitts and Nevis. The building covers about 900 square metres. It once stood right on the waterfront, but the land to the south has since been reclaimed.

It photographs well because the long stone façade, with its arches and dome, sits neatly along the street. Standing back lets you fit the whole frontage in, with the road giving you a natural foreground. The best view is from Bay Road near the Circus end, looking at the front of the building. Morning is the best time, when the façade is in full light. The building may be partly covered by scaffolding during repair work, so you may find it looks different from the usual postcard view. If so, concentrate on the parts that are visible, such as the arched entrance. Photography inside the museum is reportedly not allowed, so plan on exterior shots only.
text.geographic_location: On Bay Road in Basseterre, near the Circus end of the street. The old Treasury Building stands where the street wraps around its block.
text.directions_text: Head for the Circus end of Bay Road in Basseterre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the street so the whole façade fits with the road in the foreground. If the pavement is narrow or traffic keeps you close, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more) for the arched entrance and the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bay Road (near the Circus end, looking at the building's façade). The full colonial façade of the Old Treasury Building running along the street, shot from a distance with the street in the foreground. From here you see the full colonial façade running along the street, with the road in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's roofline level with a horizontal line. Leave some road at the bottom of the frame for depth. For a second view, walk to the arched entrance of the Old Treasury Building and look back toward the building, so the arch frames the stone façade and dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Be careful to keep a safe distance from traffic when you step back for a wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the building is in full light.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the public street, but entry to the museum and any restrictions on photography inside should be checked on the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the roofline level against a gridline helps keep a façade looking straight.
Photography inside the museum is reportedly not permitted.
The façade may be partly covered by scaffolding during repair work.

name: Basseterre Co-Cathedral of Immaculate Conception
label: Immaculate Conception
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Independence Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Independence Square' (way/24800627): middle (168 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4868078: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Twin-towered Catholic co-cathedral near Independence Square.

text.description: The Co-Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception is a Roman Catholic co-cathedral in Basseterre, and the grey stone building closes off the eastern side of Independence Square. That makes it an easy subject for a phone: a wide, open foreground with the square's fountain, and the cathedral filling the far side. Catholic worship in the town goes back to the French period, when the Jesuits built a church in the town. Catholics were later barred from worshipping in public under English rule, and the community grew again after 1829 and with settlers arriving from Madeira from 1835. A church of about 1856 was pulled down in 1927 and replaced on the same site. The present building was designed by Father Claeys and dedicated on 6 December 1928. For the classic view, start on the west side of the square and face east, with the fountain low in the frame and the cathedral behind it. Then walk over to the cathedral for a closer look at the front and the towers, where a tall traveller's palm stands beside the building. Photo guides say the interior, with its altar and stained glass, is worth a picture too. Services are held here, so go outside Mass times, keep your phone quiet and don't use flash.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Basseterre, on the east side of Independence Square, just south of North Independence Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for Basseterre, so head for Independence Square in the town centre. For the close-up view, walk over to the cathedral for a closer look at the front of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the square, fountain and cathedral together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square, or if you are close to the front and need to fit the whole facade in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Independence Square (west side of the square, facing east toward the cathedral). The grey stone cathedral filling the far side of the square, with the square's fountain in the foreground. Facing east toward the cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on a lower third line, with the cathedral's towers in the upper part of the frame. Keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean. If you want a second angle, walk over to the cathedral for a closer shot of the facade and towers, with the tall traveller's palm beside the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the grey stonework keeps its detail. Inside, use night mode only if you can hold the phone still, and keep flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not directly behind the cathedral. Outside, mornings and late afternoons are usually easier for light. Visit the interior outside service times.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the cathedral is a working place of worship with services held, so keep to non-Mass times, dress respectfully and check the official site before you go.

name: Berkeley Memorial Clock
label: Berkeley Memorial
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4892058: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Victorian clock on The Circus roundabout, styled after Piccadilly Circus.

text.description: The Berkeley Memorial is a clock and drinking fountain combined, standing in the middle of the Circus in Basseterre. It has four clock faces, one looking down each of the four streets that lead into the Circus. It was built in honour of Thomas Berkeley. The structure was designed and built by George Smith and Co. of Glasgow, Scotland. That foundry made two other similar structures, and only the one on Saint Kitts is said to have survived. That history makes it a good subject for a quick, characterful photo of the town centre. It photographs well because it is a tall, detailed shape in the middle of an open junction, with the surrounding buildings and street life behind it. Take one wide shot to show the clock in its setting, then zoom in for the clock face and the ironwork. Turn on the gridlines so the tower stands straight, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals. If people or vehicles pass through, wait a moment and take several frames.
text.geographic_location: The memorial stands in the centre of the Circus, the junction in the middle of Basseterre where four streets meet.
text.directions_text: Head for the Circus in the centre of Basseterre. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole memorial. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and the details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want the memorial and the surrounding street in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the whole structure fits comfortably in a 1x frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the memorial in the centre or just off-centre, using the gridlines to keep the sides upright. Leave a little space above the clock so the top is not cut off. Then zoom in on one clock face for a close-up. Walk round to the other sides to see the other three faces and the streets they look down.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the clock face to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and the clock looks dark. Take a few frames in case people or vehicles pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The memorial stands in the open in the centre of the Circus, but check the official site before you go if you need any access details.
claims_not_in_sources: The Circus is a public street junction where people and vehicles pass, so frames may include passing traffic.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light, and early in the day is usually quieter.
No ticket is needed to photograph the memorial from the street.

name: St. George's Anglican Church
label: St George's Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7588089: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic Anglican church with a prominent tower.

text.description:
St. George's is an Anglican parish church and Pro-Cathedral in Basseterre. French Jesuits built a church here in 1670, dedicated to Our Lady. English soldiers burned it in 1706, and it was rebuilt and renamed St. George's in 1710. The building you see today was begun in 1856 and consecrated in March 1859. Fire gutted it in 1867, and it was re-roofed and restored in 1869. Hurricanes since 1989 have damaged it again, and restoration work has followed.

For a photographer, the appeal is a historic church with a layered past, so it suits both a wide shot of the whole building and closer pictures of its details. Walk around before you decide, because the best angle depends on what is in front of you on the day. Start with a wide frame to show the church in its surroundings. Then move closer for the entrance, windows and stonework. If a service is under way, be discreet and ask before photographing inside. The church also has a pipe organ, installed in 1872 by Booth of Wakefield, which is worth a thought if you are allowed in.
text.geographic_location: St. George's Anglican Church stands in Basseterre, Saint Kitts and Nevis.
text.directions_text: If you are coming from further away, use the map to find your way to the church. The phone icon on the map is about 520 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and need to fit it all in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as the tower, windows or doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 520 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the church's vertical lines straight by holding the phone level, not tilted upwards. Take one wide shot to show the church in its setting, then move in for details. Telephoto is a good way to isolate architectural features without stepping into the road or other people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church on the screen to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its colour. If you go inside, tap on a dim area and avoid flash, as it can be disturbing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun lights the front of the church rather than shining straight at the lens. Going early or late in the day usually gives softer, more flattering light.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules about photography or dress.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and more flattering for photographing buildings.
Shooting directly into the sun can make the church dark and lose detail in the stonework.
Photography inside a working church may be restricted, so it is polite to ask first.
